tools.name: scanruler_status
tools.description: Whether a ScanRuler page is connected to this agent, which version and plugins it has, whether its tab is hidden (page.hidden), and — when none is — how the user connects one. session, with a page, says what it holds: the scan, the project’s name, whether it has changes not saved (unsaved), and its work counted — elements, features, notes … — so a session someone else left is seen before it is replaced (scan_open with saveTo keeps it). backend says whether ScanRuler runs in a tab (page) or in this server (headless). jobs lists the calls that change the session still running and the latest five others, newest first, each running, done or failed — a call whose answer you did not get is among them; scanruler_wait { for: "job", job } gives its answer, also for a job of an earlier copy of this server, which the page remembers; jobsMore counts the older ones kept. folders: where a scan or a project was opened from or saved into, the latest first — what scanruler_write writes into and scanruler_files lists; kept when the server restarts. server.answerWithin: the seconds a call is held at most before it answers with its job. server.version is this server’s, server.latest the newest on npm when known, server.handedOffFrom the older copy that started this one in its place. server.role: holder — this copy holds the port and the tab’s connection; relay — another copy (another chat or AI app) holds them and this one sends its calls through it, the work still running in the tab, server.holder.version saying which (null: from before 0.4.1); none — neither yet, server.error saying why. serverTooOld, when there, says the server the page is connected to is older than the page needs — while relaying, the holding copy, not this one: tell the person once, in its words, and install nothing yourself. tools, when there, says the tools you were given are not the ones the page offers now (stale): which were added, removed or changed — named the first time, counted after — and which page they were listed from.

tools.name: scanruler_open
tools.description: Open ScanRuler in the user’s default browser, paired with this server, and wait for the page to connect — for when scanruler_status says none is. The first time, the browser asks the user whether the site may reach apps on this computer; they must allow it. Returns the status, with opened: whether the browser was asked to open it. If connected is still false, tell the user what howToConnect says.

tools.name: scanruler_wait
tools.description: Wait until a ScanRuler page is connected (for: "page", the default), or until it is also done with what it is busy with and every change still running has finished (for: "idle" — then finished lists the changes done or failed since the last such answer, a failed one with its error, and state says idle or running), or until a job is done (for: "job" with job — a call started with wait: false, one answered queued, or one whose answer did not come; scanruler_status lists them). Returns the status — for idle only connected, state and finished — or for a job its answer: { job, tool, state, ms, result } or { …, error: { code, message } } — state running if the time ran out first: call it again. A job of an earlier copy of this server is read from the page's record of it (session.recent), from says so. It waits 45 s at most, this server's answer limit, whatever timeoutSeconds says. connected is false if the time ran out waiting for a page.

job.description: The job to wait for, with for: "job" — as a call with wait: false, a queued answer or scanruler_status gave it.

timeoutSeconds.description: How long to wait at most, seconds — 120 by default, and never past 45.

tools.name: scanruler_write
tools.description: Write a text file — a report, notes, a table of readings — next to the scan, as UTF-8: .md, .txt, .csv, .json only, and only inside the folder this server last opened a scan or a project from (scan_open, project_load) or saved one into (saveTo), or a folder under it. A relative path is taken in that folder; an absolute one must lie in one of those folders, and a path may not climb out with "..". A file already there is replaced. Returns its path and size in bytes. Refused while this server has opened no scan or project from a folder — then open the scan with scan_open first, or write the file yourself.

path.description: The file: a name in the scan’s folder ("report.md"), a path under it ("report/sigma.md"), or an absolute path in it — .md, .txt, .csv, .json.

text.description: What the file holds, as text.

tools.name: scanruler_files
tools.description: The files in the folder this server last opened a scan or a project from, or saved one into — kept when the server restarts — or in a folder under it (path): each file's name, size in bytes and kind (mesh, project, step, picture, drawing, text or other), newest first, and the folders in it. Where scanruler_write's reports and the files saved beside the scan are; up to 300 entries. Refused while no scan or project has been opened from a folder.

path.description: A folder under the scan’s folder, relative to it or absolute; or one of the folders scanruler_status lists. Leave out for the scan’s folder.

tools.name: scanruler_batch
tools.description: Run several of the ScanRuler tools in one call, in order, each with its own arguments — a run of scan_nearest, element_fit or section_get calls, say. Returns results, one per call in order: { tool, ok, result } or { tool, ok: false, error: { code, message } }. The first refused stops the rest (stopped says which index, failed: { index, tool, error } which call) unless stopOnError is false. When the refused call is a change, then with rollback (the default) every change the batch made before it is undone, so the batch stands or falls whole: undone names the steps taken back, newest first. A refused read — section_get, scan_query, any tool that changes nothing — undoes nothing: what came before it stands (kept says so). A call refused busy is run again once the page is idle (retried: "busy" on its result). Each call that changes the session is still its own undo step. build: "end" builds a modelled part once for a run of changes to it — sketches edited one after another, say — rather than after each: every call but the last is sent deferred, and a change so sent answers before its rebuild (build: "held", its result and bodies the part as last built; a pick by index names a face of that part); the last call builds them all, and so does a read of the part, or any other kind of tool, met on the way. timings: true gives each call its ms and the batch total_ms, and a change's build the steps it played with their ms (result.steps.played). wait: false answers at once with { queued, job }, and so does a batch still running at the server’s answer limit (with after, its seconds); scanruler_wait { for: "job", job } gives the batch's answer. A { "$file": path } anywhere in a call’s arguments is that JSON file’s contents. A tool that returns a picture is not shown here: the picture is written to a file — its call’s path, or a new file in /pkg — and its result gives that file.path; call the tool directly to see the picture. The server’s own tools (scanruler_status, _open, _wait, _batch, _write, _files, _tools) cannot be batched.

calls.description: The calls, in order — or give file instead.

tool.description: A tool’s name, as listed — scan_nearest, element_fit.

arguments.description: Its arguments, as the tool takes them; {} for none.

file.description: A JSON file of the calls, read here in place of calls: [{ tool, arguments }], or [{ name, input }] by the command's own name (scan.open), or either under "calls" or "steps". For a long run a script wrote, which then need not pass through the conversation. A relative path is taken from /pkg.

stopOnError.description: Stop at the first refused call (the default), or run every call and report each.

rollback.description: When the batch stops at a refused change, undo what it changed before it (the default) — or leave those changes standing (false). A refused read undoes nothing either way.

build.description: each (the default): a change rebuilds the part before it answers. end: the changes build once, at the last call.

timings.description: Each call’s ms, the batch’s total_ms, and the steps a change’s build played with their ms.

wait.description: false: answer at once with { queued: true, job } while the call runs on; scanruler_wait { for: "job", job } gives its answer. true (the default): answer once it is done — or, still running at the server’s answer limit (scanruler_status: server.answerWithin, seconds), with { queued: true, job, after } all the same.

tools.name: align_datum
tools.description: A 3-2-1 alignment, as the panel’s alignment box sets it up: primary levels the part — a plane (or 3 points on a face) whose outward normal becomes primaryAxis (default z-, the face the part stands on facing down); secondary turns it — a line or an axis (or 2 points along an edge) laid along secondaryAxis (default x+), or a plane, whose outward NORMAL goes on secondaryAxis, not along it (a side wall as secondary with x+ ends up facing x+), turned square to the primary; origin is the zero point — a point, sphere or circle (or 1 point). Each is an element by id or name, or points in mm: points are used as given, not snapped to the scan (an origin point is the zero exactly where it is; scan.nearest puts a point on the surface first). Each datum zeroes the coordinates it owns (a plane the one along its normal, an axis or line the two across it); the origin sets only the coordinates they leave open — with a plane and a line, the one along the line. An origin alone moves the part without turning it, all three coordinates. Everything measured moves with the part. On the part’s first alignment the coordinates nothing sets are centred on the scan’s box centre; keepFree: true leaves them where they are. Returns the transform applied — the whole alignment the part carries, when it was aligned before — how many elements moved with it, centred (the coordinates centred, as ["y"]), with an origin which coordinates it set and where its point now stands (a note when that is off zero), and parallelFace when a face parallel to a levelling plane and within 5 mm of it holds more of the scan (its offset along the plane’s outward normal, how many times the area, a note) — the part may stand on that one. One undo step.

Returns the alignment (RMS, points matched, transform) and the map’s statistics. One undo step.

tools.name: deviation_export
tools.description: The deviation map as a file of readings, for working on it elsewhere: side "scan" (the default) a reading per scan vertex — its place in the frame the scan is measured in (what scan.query gives) and its signed distance from the reference part, or from the element deviation.set_target measures against; side "reference" a reading per sample of the map on the reference (deviation.settings { on: "reference" } — measured if it is not yet), in the reference’s frame, positive where the reference stands outside the scan. format: ply (the default; binary, float x, y, z, deviation and uchar measured), npy (an N × 4 float32 array x, y, z, d, for numpy.load) or csv (x,y,z,d, for a spreadsheet). The distance is NaN ("nan" in the CSV) where there is no reading; a reading past the search distance is kept as it is — the map draws it bare and the statistics leave it out, so measured is 0 on it (PLY), and in the others |d| ≤ searchDistance says it counts. Returns the file and the figures to check it by: readings, measured, withinTolerance and withinTolerancePct (of the measured, ± tolerance — on the scan’s side what the deviation state’s stats give; on the reference’s, by reading, where the state gives it by area), tolerance and searchDistance. Changes nothing. The file is written to `path`; the result says where and how large it is, not its bytes.

side.description: The readings: per scan vertex (the default), or per sample on the reference.

path.description: Where to write the file: a file path, or a folder to write it into under the name ScanRuler gives it. Without it, it goes into /pkg.

tools.name: deviation_hotspots
tools.description: The deviation map read as patches: the scan vertices whose deviation lies past the tolerance (the map’s own, under deviation.settings, unless tolerance says otherwise) gathered into connected regions, the largest and farthest first — where the part is off, how large each place is and by how much, instead of one number over the whole part. Each patch: its centre and box in mm (in the frame the scan is measured in — what scan.query { box } and element.fit take), its area, how many vertices, the mean and the extreme deviation and which side (outside the reference or inside), the point of the extreme and the scan vertex there, and a few of its vertices (what element.fit_marked takes). With a map against the reference part the patch’s centre and extreme are given on the reference too (onReference — what the Deviation workspace shows and view.render { frame } takes there). grain is how close two vertices over tolerance have to be to be one patch, three point spacings by default. found and over say how many patches and vertices over tolerance there were in all — within the search distance, the vertices the map draws as a measurement. Then far, the vertices past the search distance, which the map draws bare: read it every time — far.inside is the scan deeper inside the reference than the search distance, where the reference has material the part has not (a hole, a pocket or a slot the model lacks), far.outside the scan further off it, where the part has what the model has not, or scan spray; each with its count and its patches, the largest first, and far.count both together; unmeasured says how many vertices the facing limit left without a reading. Needs a deviation map (deviation.align, or deviation.set_target). on: "reference" reads the map on the reference instead (deviation.settings { on }, measured if it is not yet): the patches are of the reference, in its frame, outside where the reference stands proud of the scan (material the part has not) and inside where it is short of it; far is the reference past the search distance from the scan, by side; and noScan, the reference with no scan behind it, in patches the largest first — surface the model has on no evidence: inferred, unscanned, or not on the part. Changes nothing.

tolerance.description: ± mm; the map’s tolerance by default.

patches.description: How many patches to name; 8 by default, 50 at most.

grain.description: mm — how close two vertices over tolerance have to be to be one patch; three point spacings by default.

on.description: The map read: on the scan (the default) or on the reference.

annotations.title: Where the deviation lies over tolerance

tools.name: deviation_settings
tools.description: The deviation map’s reading: range, the colour scale ± mm; maxDistance, how far from the reference a point may be to count, mm; bands, a stepped scale of that many colours or null for smooth; tolerance, ± mm, the share within which the statistics give; facingDeg, how far the reference surface a point is measured against may turn from facing it, degrees, or null for the nearest surface whatever it faces — a change of it measures the map again; colormap, the colour map every deviation map and the live map of the bodies are drawn in — the person’s own choice, kept in the browser and outside the undo, so set it only to read a render by its colours and read settings.colormap for what the ramp shows at −range, 0 and +range and the caps past either end before judging a picture; on, which surface a map against the reference part is painted on — "scan" (the scan by its distance to the reference, the default) or "reference" (the reference by its distance to the scan, measured the first time it is asked for: positive where the reference stands outside the scan — material the part has not, a boss or a wall the model has and the scan does not — negative where it is short of it, grey where no scan stands behind it, a reading past the search distance in the cap of its end). Read both: the scan’s side finds what the model lacks, the reference’s what the model has that the part has not, and how much of the model no scan supports (onReference.noScanPct in the state). show, the map switch (the view bar’s Map key): false leaves the surface bare to look at its shape, the map still measured and read — the figures, hotspots and pins go on; true paints it again; a project keeps it, so read settings.show in the state when a render comes out uncoloured. view.render pictures the side on screen, and says which map it painted (map) or why none (mapWhy). Returns the deviation state. One undo step.

tools.name: dimension_add
tools.description: Measure between elements, or a size or tolerance of one, as the panel’s dimension box does. refs are the elements by id or name — a section by its id or name counts as the plane it was cut on. Without type, the type follows the elements as clicking them in the viewport does — two spheres or points give their centre distance, two planes their distance, a plane and an axis their distance, and so on. With type, it is one of: dist-point-point (From, To); dist-point-axis (Point, Axis); dist-point-plane (Point, Plane); dist-axis-axis (Axis A, Axis B); dist-axis-plane (Axis, Plane); dist-plane-plane (From, To); angle-axis-axis (Axis A, Axis B); angle-axis-plane (Axis, Plane); angle-plane-plane (Plane A, Plane B); size-diameter (Feature); form-flatness (Plane); form-cylindricity (Cylinder); form-circularity (Circle); form-sphericity (Sphere); orient-parallelism (Feature, Datum); orient-perpendicularity (Feature, Datum); orient-angularity (Feature, Datum); loc-coaxiality (Feature, Datum axis). anchor, for two spheres: center (default), gap or span. limit holds the value to a ceiling or a nominal ± band. Returns the dimension with its value (mm or degrees, finer than the panel shows it), the formatted value the panel shows, and the verdict. One undo step.

workspace.description: For text: whose report — measure (the default), deviation, thickness or flat.

tools.name: scan_draft
tools.description: The scan’s walls that run near a pull direction — the sides a mould opens along, a side core slides along — gathered into patches, each with the angle it leans off the pull: draftDeg, positive where the wall faces partly along the pull (it lets go as the tool moves that way), negative where it faces back (a back draft, an undercut to that pull); sigmaDeg its standard error, spreadDeg the points’ own spread (mostly the scan’s normal noise); with centroid, box, area (mm²), count, facing (which way the wall faces across the pull) and turnDeg (how far that turns across the patch). Neighbouring walls are parted where the way they face jumps, so a box’s four sides are four patches, and a thin wall’s two sides (a blade, a rib) two patches facing opposite ways; a point joins a patch only while it faces within 20° of the patch’s mean, so a smooth freeform wall comes in patches that turn 40° at most. A boss’s or a hole’s round side is one patch with round: true, its facing no one way. Read it early on a moulded or cast part, along each direction the tools open: walls that lean half a degree to a few explain fits that miss by the lean. pull: the direction, any length; box: only the scan inside it; nearDeg: how far off square to the pull a wall may lean and still count (10 by default); patches: how many, the largest first (12); minArea: smaller ones left out, mm² (1); split: no patch reaches across this plane — "symmetry" (the scan’s mirror plane: the last measured symmetry plane, else searched for), a plane element, "XY", "YZ", "ZX", or { point, normal } — each patch then says its side (1 along the plane’s normal, −1 against), and the answer the plane. Changes nothing.

pull.description: The pull direction, any length — the way the tool opens.

box.description: Only the scan inside this box.

split.description: Keep every patch to one side of this plane.

annotations.title: Read the draft against a pull

tools.name: scan_fit_surface
tools.description: A patch of the scan measured as a surface — a sloped side, a twisted ruled face, a dome, a saddle, a fairing — the points given as vertices (from scan.query or a patch) or as a box (normal keeps those facing a way, within withinDeg, 30 by default). The best plane through them sets the patch’s own frame: origin at their centroid, normal (w) out of it, basisU and basisV in it, all in the frame the part is measured in now. Each model is a height over (u, v) along the normal: plane h = a + b·u + c·v; bilinear + d·u·v (a hyperbolic paraboloid: a straight-lined twisted face); quadric + d·u² + e·u·v + f·v² (a dome, bowl, saddle or a cylinder’s strip). Each answers its coefficients, rms and worst (mm off along the normal); the quadric also curvature: k1 and k2 (1/mm, the larger first), r1 and r2 (their radii, null where flat), axis1 and axis2 (their directions in the world) and shape (flat, cylinder, dome or saddle) at the patch’s middle. model: one of them, or best (the default) — every one, and best names the simplest whose rms is within a tenth of the lowest: the model that holds, plain. At most limit points are fitted (20000), spread evenly. Changes nothing.

vertices.description: The scan vertices of the patch.

box.description: The patch as the scan inside a box, in place of vertices.

normal.description: With box: only the vertices facing this way.

model.description: Which surface; best (the default) fits each and names the simplest that holds.

limit.description: How many points at most; 20000 by default.

annotations.title: Fit a sloped or curved patch

tools.name: scan_heightmap
tools.description: Where the scan is first met looking along an axis, or square onto a plane, over a grid of cells: pocket floors, ledges, a step's height, a face's tilt, a pad's tiers, an icon on a key in one call. axis is the way looked: -z (the default) looks down from above and gives the top surface's z; +z looks up from below and gives the underside's; ±x, ±y likewise. Cells lie on the two other axes in order — x, y for z; y, z for x; x, z for y — as u and v. plane, in place of axis: a plane element (id or name; its normal turned to the side the scan is not, so it looks at the face it was fitted on), a coordinate plane "XY", "YZ", "ZX", or any other — a face of a model, say — as { origin, normal, u? }; the map then looks down the normal onto it, height is the distance from the plane along the normal, and u, v are the plane's own, laid as a sketch on that plane has them (section.render { plane } draws the same sheet) — u seeds its direction; flip turns the plane over. The answer's plane gives its frame in world: a cell's point is origin + u·U + v·V + height·normal. box: the part looked at, the scan's box by default; rays start at its face and stop at the far one. With plane, box is in the plane's frame: min and max are [u, v, height], and by default it takes in the whole scan. of: height (the default); deviation — the scan's signed deviation where each ray lands (the map deviation.align or deviation.set_target measured, read off the triangle met), null where the map has no reading within its search distance; relief — the height less the surface round it (at each cell a plane fitted to its neighbours, weighed by a Gaussian smooth mm wide, three cells by default; make it about the width of what is looked for): icons, grooves, lettering and parting lines stand out of a face that curves or leans, positive proud and negative sunk. cell: mm (by default a round size that makes 40 cells on the longer side; widened to keep 1600 cells at most — and 160 and 25600 when the numbers are not returned). Returns along, across, cell, origin [u0, v0] (the grid's low corner), cols, rows and grid: rows of values (mm; heights to 0.01, deviation and relief to 0.001) from the low v up, null where there is none — grid[r][c] stands at u0 + (c + ½)·cell, v0 + (r + ½)·cell — with min, max, hit (cells met) and valued (cells with a value). levels: true returns, in place of the grid, the values gathered into levels — a pad's tiers, a pocket's floor, the face round them — the largest first (12 at most): each its height (the median), sigma, range, cells, area (mm²), sharePct of the cells counted, and box ([u, v] min and max). Of a height, the cells sloped more than slopeDeg (10° by default; 90 keeps every one) are left out first and counted as sloped — a fillet's ramp, a cone, a wall met at a glance — so two tiers a ramp joins stay two levels; a face that leans more is read by looking square onto it (plane). Two levels lie at least gap apart (mm; three times the cell-to-cell noise on the cells counted by default, 0.02 at least), and unassigned counts the cells counted that fall in none (walls, edges). grid: true keeps the grid as well, false leaves it out and returns the picture. picture: true adds the map coloured by its values with coordinates in the margins and a scale (a deviation in the workspace's colour map over its range); needs the browser. Changes nothing. The picture comes back as an image; with `path` it is written to a file too, and with `inline: false` only there.

max.description: The highest corner, mm — [u, v, height] with plane.

A reference part opened from a file stays, its alignment and maps gone (referenceKept names it); one the app made from the session’s own work goes with that work (referenceDropped). Returns the scan: name, units, vertex and triangle counts, its bounding box (min and max corners), the box’s centre and its diagonal (size), in millimetres. Not undoable: a new scan starts a new history. The file is read from `path` on this computer and streamed to the page. With `saveTo`, the session is saved as a project file there first (as project_save does), then replaced as with discard: true — one call to keep what a page holds and start anew.

units.description: What the file’s coordinates are in: mm (the default), cm, m or in. An STL carries no units of its own; PLY and OBJ are taken in millimetres unless told otherwise. Everything is measured in millimetres once read.

discard.description: Replace the session even though it holds measurements — they are lost (a project file saved before keeps them). Without it the command refuses when there is work to lose.

tools.name: scan_outline
tools.description: The scan’s outline seen along an axis, or square onto a plane, read as a sketch would draw it: a flange’s plan, a bezel’s opening, a gasket’s shape. Rays over a grid of cells (half the tolerance, widened to keep 250000 at most) find where the scan is and where it is not; the line between is traced round and each loop read as the fewest lines and arcs that follow it within tolerance (mm, 0.2 by default): straight sides are fitted as lines and met at sharp corners; an arc between two sides is that corner’s round (rounds: at, the corner’s index in points, radius and center); any other arc is a side of its own (arcs: from, the index of the point it starts at, running to the next, radius and center) — a slot’s ends; and a loop that is round all the way is one circle. axis, plane, flip and box as scan.heightmap takes them — the coordinates are u, v as it lays them (the two other axes in order, or the plane’s own). Returns loops, the largest first (loops: how many, 4 by default): each with hole (true for one inside another), area (mm²), box, points ([u, v] corners in order), rounds and arcs, or circle { center, radius, rms }, and worst — how far the traced outline strays from what is drawn, mm, with worstAt where, when it is past the tolerance. Changes nothing.

axis.description: The way looked: -z (the default) from above, and so on.

tools.name: scan_pattern
tools.description: Rotational repeats about an axis — a fan's blades, a flange's holes and pads, a wheel's spokes, a gear's teeth — counted from the scan. The scan is cut square to the axis at each height in at, and each cut (only what lies between radius.min and radius.max) is turned against itself: count, the number of copies whose outlines land on each other going round (up to maxCount, 60 by default); pitchDeg, 360/count; phaseDeg, where the first copy's middle lies (under one pitch), and betweenDeg midway to the next — angles about the axis as section.cut { across: { axis, angleDeg } } takes them: 0° the coordinate axis next round (X about Z), turning by the right hand. score, 0 to 1, is how well the copies' outlines land on each other; under 0.5 nothing is taken to repeat and count is 1 (tried gives the best count and its score). Each copy in instances: angleDeg and radius of its outline's middle, offDeg from where an even spacing puts it, rms and worst — how far its outline lies from the other copies' turned onto it (the median over them), mm — and share, its outline's length against the median copy's (well under 1: the scan misses part of it, or the copy is not there). rms, worst and worstInstance over all the copies. Round outlines about the axis — a bore, a hub, a rim — are not copies: they come back as rings, each its radius, off (how far its centre lies off the axis, mm), towardDeg (which way) and rms. axis: a cylinder, cone, line or circle element, by id or name, a coordinate axis "X", "Y" or "Z" through the origin, or { origin, dir }. at: heights along the axis, mm, counted from the world origin's foot on it (the coordinate itself on a coordinate axis); by default 6 spread over the scan, 12 at most. Features lie at different heights and radii: cut through each, and keep radius to the ring one lies in where two share a height — in one cut the feature with the most outline sets the count, and the other reads as what its copies miss (worst). instances: false leaves the copies out. Changes nothing.

A cylinder, cone, line or circle element, or a coordinate axis "X", "Y", "Z".

origin.description: A point on the axis, mm.

axis.description: The axis the copies repeat round.

at.description: Heights to cut at; 6 spread over the scan by default.

radius.description: Only the cut between these distances from the axis.

maxCount.description: The most copies looked for; 60 by default.

tools.name: scan_qa
tools.description: One call before modelling, to know what the scan will and will not give: rims — the open edges of its holes (count, total length, the longest few with their number rim, length, centre and size, mm; circles: other rims a circle fits — a hole the scan did not see into); a rim that lies on a circle has circle { center, axis, radius, rms } (rms its scatter off the circle, mm), and element.fit { kind: "circle", rim } makes it an element; noise — the median scatter of small plane fits round a sample of vertices (mm; near 0 is a CAD tessellation) and its 90th percentile; thickness through the part along axis (x, y, z or a direction; by default the alignment’s z when the part is aligned, else the way most of the surface faces — a plate’s faces) over a grid — p5, p50, p95 (mm), and on the cells near the median (the main faces) the thickness’s linear trend as tiltDeg, how far apart faces that should be parallel are, with the way it thickens and its run from end to end; faces gives each face’s own tilt off square to the axis (topDeg, bottomDeg), so a lean of the whole part shows apart from faces out of parallel. notes: what looks wrong, plainly. Changes nothing.

tools.name: scan_query
tools.description: The scan’s vertices inside a box, or within a radius of a point, with their outward normals — the points on a face, to measure a dimension or a draft angle off, or to see what the scan has where a model is being built. normal keeps only the vertices facing a direction (within withinDeg, 30 by default): the top face alone, say. At most limit come back (1000 by default, 20000 at most): past it every k-th matching vertex is kept, spread evenly, and step says which k. Returns how many matched, the vertices kept (their numbers, as scan.nearest and element.fit_marked name them), their points and normals in millimetres, in the frame the part is measured in now, the box round the points kept, their centroid and mean normal. fields: count gives the numbers alone, without the vertices, points and normals; ids adds the vertices; all everything — the default, but with mark, where count is. mark: true leaves every vertex that matched marked — all of them, not the limit’s thinned list; marked.points counts them — for element.fit_marked { marked: true } and whatever else takes the marked points, so the list need not come back at all. Changes nothing on the part.

box.description: A box in the frame the part is measured in now.

near.description: A ball about a point — in place of box.

withinDeg.description: How far from it a normal may lean, degrees; 30 by default.

With them the plane (origin, normal, basisU, basisV: a sheet point is origin + u·basisU + v·basisV), and for each chain whether it is closed (a loop; its first point is repeated at the end), its length along the path, how many points it has and the box round it on the sheet. tools.name: section_render
tools.description: A picture of a section as a PNG, for checking a slice against what was built on it: the scan’s cut as points on the section’s sheet ([u, v] mm as section.get gives them, +u right, +v up), a grid ruled in millimetres with its values at the top and left margins — world coordinates where the sheet’s u or v runs along a world axis, sheet mm otherwise — the world direction across and up named in the margins (axes in the answer: per sheet axis the world axis it runs nearest, offDeg and, along it, at0, the world coordinate at the sheet’s 0), a scale bar, and over it what the workspaces’ layers draw — a model’s cut by the section’s plane as outlines, a sketch’s pieces with their ids where the sketch lies in that plane, whatever it was drawn on. Every scan point within ten tolerances of an outline is read against it: on it within ± tolerance (grey), or off it (red), outside the outline or inside it; points with no outline near are pale. The answer gives gap: points (the cut’s), read, over (red), outside and inside (of a closed outline — inside is scan within the model’s material, so the model stands proud there; outside, the model is short), max and rms (mm) and overBox (the sheet box round the red, to frame the next look); layers: each layer drawn by key, its outlines and pieces counted; map: picture pixel (column c, row r from the top) is the sheet place [left + c·unitsPerPx, top − r·unitsPerPx]. section names a section; or plane cuts the scan for the picture alone — no section is made, and the sheet is a sketch’s on that plane: zero at the world origin’s foot, u along the coordinate axis next round from the normal (YZ: u = Y, v = Z; ZX: u = Z, v = X; XY: u = X, v = Y), so on a coordinate plane [u, v] are world coordinates (the answer’s sheet gives them). plane is { origin, normal }, an element by id or name (the plane through its centre square to its direction — a plane element’s normal, a cylinder’s axis — on the sheet a sketch on it takes, not the fitter’s own axes), or { sketch } by id or name: the scan cut on that sketch’s plane, in its own frame, so [u, v] are its pieces’. A section’s own sheet counts from the part’s centre instead. up: "x", "y" or "z" turns the picture’s sheet in its plane so that world axis runs up it — a side view with Z up: v is that axis laid into the plane, u the direction square to it running + to the right, the plane seen from whichever side gives that (the ZX plane with up "z": u = X, v = Z, seen from −Y, as a front view; a section’s sheet keeps its zero) — and everything the picture says in [u, v] (frame, map, overBox, axes) is then on that turned sheet, which the answer gives as sheet. Without up the sheet lies as above. offsets: 2 to 9 cuts in one picture — the section’s or plane’s slid along its normal by each, mm — side by side, each tile labelled with its offset, all on one frame and scale (the square round every cut unless frame is given); the answer gives per tile its offset, origin and gap, and map.tile and map.cols (map holds for each tile from its own corner). frame { at: [u, v], size } looks at a square of the sheet; everything by default. tolerance: the Deviation workspace’s by default. layers: the keys to draw; every one by default, [] for the scan alone. 800 px on the long side by default, up to 2048. instructions: These tools drive ScanRuler, a measuring app for 3D scans, in the browser tab the user has open: the user watches every step in the viewport and can undo it there. Start with scanruler_status. If no ScanRuler page is connected, call scanruler_open: it opens ScanRuler in the user’s browser, paired with this server, and waits for it. If that leaves it unconnected, tell the user what howToConnect says, then call scanruler_wait. Before a task’s first step, read its guide with guide_read — how to measure a scan, model a part or turn a scan into CAD, written for the ScanRuler build connected: guide_read with no topic lists the guides and their sections. Read session_state before acting and after: the scan’s bounding box says where the part lies, the elements and dimensions what is measured. Lengths are millimetres, angles degrees; answers give numbers to six significant digits. A place on the scan is { point: [x, y, z] } (the nearest scan vertex is taken) or { vertex: n }. To fit a feature, aim at its middle, not at an edge. Every tool that changes the session is one step of the undo history; history_undo takes the last back. report_get gives the report as JSON (format "json") or as the text the panel copies (format "text"). A change, a batch or a long read still running at the server’s answer limit (scanruler_status: server.answerWithin) answers { queued: true, job } and runs on: scanruler_wait { for: "job", job } gives its answer — call it again while it says running. view_render shows you the 3D view as a picture; view_set turns it to a standard view or fits it. scanruler_batch runs several tools in one call, in order — many scan_nearest or element_fit calls, say — and stops at the first that is refused unless told to go on.
